title: Visual Jev: Accurate and Efficient Decisions from Shared Visual Context
authors: Guanxu Yu; Yuhang Yao
main_finding: Post-training raised equal-weight macro accuracy from 0.706 to 0.761; with 32 questions per image, shared batched execution was 8.9× faster (warm, amortized) than independent serial calls and 3.4× faster than batching that recomputes the prefix.
caveats: 5.7 ms is amortized: a 32-question batch completes in about 182 ms. It is not the latency of an independent request.; Accuracy gains concentrate on the two task families represented in training.; A matched typed head showed no consistent accuracy advantage over the LM-head readout.; Single-machine study on a consumer GPU; queueing latency is excluded.

title: REFLEX with Jev for Efficient Selective Control in LLM Agents
authors: Tiantong Wu; Wei Yang Bryan Lim
main_finding: At threshold τ = 0.5, REFLEX reached 95% success with 1.12 strong-model calls per task, against 88% and 4.10 calls for the strong-only agent (72.7% fewer strong calls).
caveats: Only one proprietary decision model is tested.; On BFCL ordinary routing is near-saturated; on τ-style episodes a cheap generative cascade remains competitive.; The τ evaluation is a 300-episode held-out validation, not a full leaderboard; API costs are dated snapshots.; Action-set size and ambiguity effects concentrate in authority and risk families.

title: JEV-as-a-Judge: Accept When Confident, Escalate When Unsure
authors: Yubo Li; Yidi Miao; Ramayya Krishnan; Rema Padman
main_finding: Jev came within three points of GPT-6 wherever the verdict could be read off the text, at 0.36% of its fee and a 0.15 s median latency, and fell behind where the verdict had to be derived (math, code, logic). A cascade with a threshold frozen in advance beat GPT-6 by 0.9 points on 1,610 held-out pairs at 41% of its fee, and in a pre-specified live test on two new workloads it matched GPT-6’s accuracy exactly.
caveats: Comparators were added in rounds after initial results were known; only the frozen policies, the primary adjudication and the prospective test were fixed in advance.; Human adjudication covers 183 disagreement-selected items annotated by one team member.; Latency comes from one client location; apart from the live test, cascade fees and latencies are simulated offline.; Confidence routing weakens on style-adversarial pairs and reference-free prose.

title: Type-Safe Is Not Error-Free: A Constrained Decision Head Follows the Option Name, Not the Rubric Bound to It
authors: Yu Sun; Junhao Xu
main_finding: Rebinding the rubrics behind no/yes lowered hosted Jev’s AUROC from .8146 to .5806 and flipped 32.50% of its answers (neutral names: ~2%; 24× its test–retest floor) while type errors stayed at 0%. The steeper .94→.23 inversion comes from an open marker head, not from Jev.
caveats: The .9376→.2315 AUROC inversion belongs to an open marker-readout checkpoint, not to hosted Jev.; One released checkpoint per open read-out geometry; English only.; The hosted model is a non-deterministic black box observed at one point in time; no model version is pinned.; The multi-way arm rests on a pool with shipped accuracy .5637 and is directional.; Mitigations (neutral identifiers; randomising names in training) are proposed, not evaluated.

title: Open-Jev Judgments on CallScreenBench: Calibrated One-Pass Scam Screening with a Small Language Model
authors: Simiao Ren; Kidus Zewde; Xingyu Shen; Yuchen Zhou; Dennis Ng; Ankit Raj; Tommy Duong; Yuxin Zhang; Neo Tiangratanakul
main_finding: A three-seed ensemble reached AUROC .974 with calibration error .052, non-inferior to an LLM judge at a pre-registered .02 margin, with no false alarms on legitimate calls and decisions 1.14 turns earlier; 64.5 ms per decision on one consumer GPU, 4.9× faster than the same backbone fine-tuned to generate.
caveats: Recipe selection had test-set exposure (about ten recipes were scored before the selection rule was fixed).; A fine-tuned ModernBERT encoder is not significantly worse; the gain is in readout and calibration, not accuracy.; All callers are synthetic.; Single-model latency and the three-model ensemble quality are measured on different scopes.

title: Jev-Mem: System-One-Controlled Agentic Memory for Efficient AI Agents
authors: Dongming Jiang; Yi Li; Bingzhe Li
main_finding: LLM-as-a-Judge 0.777 on LoCoMo (+11.0% relative to the strongest baseline), memory construction in 158 s (6.6× faster than the fastest competing system) and 0.93 s average query latency (36.7% lower).
caveats: Each headline number is relative to a different baseline.; Gains belong to the full memory system, not to Jev alone; module-level attribution is needed.; The quality metric is itself an LLM judge; transfer to other datasets is untested.; No Jev model version is pinned.

title: Calibrated Decisions at Scale: Converting Police Crash Narratives into Probabilistic Crash Variables with a System One Model (Jev)
authors: Amir Rafe; Subasish Das
main_finding: Against human labels the typed model reached F1 0.908; one frontier model was 0.059 higher and the other indistinguishable. Probabilities ranked well but overstated prevalence; recalibration on the same labels cut calibration error about 3.3×.
caveats: Single region, single model version and single schema.; Recalibration was fitted on labels from the same distribution; it is not a guarantee for new regions or schemas.; Two-decimal output probabilities put a floor on calibration error for rare variables.; Narratives and record-level files are not redistributable; a de-identified audit table is available on request once the data owner confirms.

title: JEVQA - Video Quality from Metadata, Bitstream, and Pixel Features with a General-Purpose Decision Model
authors: Werner Robitza
main_finding: With metadata only, JEVQA reached PLCC 0.737 against VMAF (P.1204.1: 0.733), rising to 0.797 with bitstream data and 0.824 with bitstream plus pixel features; against MOS it reached 0.879 (P.1204.1: 0.898).
caveats: Study A’s target is VMAF, not human MOS.; Trained models on the same features remain clearly ahead in both studies; the pixel-only variant failed.; Standard models have seen part of the Study B database.; Feature extraction does the perceptual work; this does not show that Jev can watch video.

title: Evaluating Decision Models for Text Annotation in Computational Social Science
authors: Hazem Ibrahim; Yasir Zaki
main_finding: Jev trailed the per-task best LLM on 14 of 15 tasks (median −11.6 macro-F1) at a median 44× lower measured cost. Its median ECE (0.157) beat the verbalised confidence of 16 of 19 LLMs but not three frontier Claude models (best 0.066). Routing low-confidence items to an LLM matched or exceeded the LLM alone at a quarter to half of its cost.
caveats: High confidence is not reliable across constructs: on empathy the model is confident while performing near chance (task calibration error 0.538).; Verbalised LLM confidence and native probabilities are different signals; baselines that decline to estimate are excluded from calibration.; Older public corpora may overlap with training data; the overlap is unknown.

title: Jev for Scientific Decisions: Evaluating Semantic Choices and Their Consequences
authors: Boyuan Deng; Shuyi Fan; Hongyang Zhang; Xinhong Xie
main_finding: Jev matched five other configurations at complete semantic correctness and had the lowest observed median latency among successful responses (0.335 s; p95 0.442 s). Seven wrong selections by comparison models changed downstream counts while leaving the final label correct.
caveats: A tiny development collection; repetitions do not add independent cases.; Every model-routed reference label is “inconsistent”, so balanced claim decisions are untested.; All observed semantic errors concern a single Choice.

title: this-that-model-1.0: A typed decision model that decides in 30 ms, for a millionth of a cent
authors: Zehua Cheng; Wei Dai; Jiahao Sun
main_finding: 30.9 ms per decision on one laptop GPU; on the 68-question cohort 0.941 accuracy (Brier 0.042) against Jev’s 0.765 (0.133); on the 2,250-question subset 0.844 against Jev’s 0.803.
caveats: The 68-question accuracy gap rests on 12 questions.; The model was trained on the 2,250-question subset’s question shapes; Jev was not.; Electricity-only marginal cost excludes hardware and operations and is not comparable to an API price.; Weaker than strong reasoning models on multi-step arithmetic; on branch-shaped families 0.818 against 0.837–0.968 for hosted models.

title: Replacing Large Language Models with Jev Decision Models for Low-Latency Edge Service Orchestration
short_title: Replacing LLMs with Jev at the Edge
authors: Delong Li; Xu Wang; Haochen Gong; Rui Lang; Guangsheng Yu
main_finding: Across 33 conditions Jev cut median decision latency by 22.7–64.5% against the fastest LLM, almost independently of input size, contract width or catalog size; on four-field contracts its fees per correct decision were 59.7–80.9% lower at a cost of a few exact-match points, and on the live admission path it kept 0.91–0.95 of requests exact and on time where the LLMs fell below 0.1.
caveats: Wide contracts mark the limit of the substitution.; Caching repeated descriptions gives all interpreters nearly the same latency: the gain lies in fresh decisions.; Same author group as 2609.23136 and 2610.06425.

title: Intent Interpretation at RIC Timescales: Jev Decision Models versus Large Language Models in 6G Open RAN

caveats: One common-random-number realization per design point.; Same author group as 2609.22753 and 2610.06425.

caveats: Only two held-out human-referenced datasets test the hybrid; two preregistered primary endpoints were not shown.; Corrections can import the flagship’s errors.; The Jev response cache is not released, and vendor updates prevent guaranteed regeneration of outputs.; Single-author work with recent code.

title: Decision Hijacking: Prompt Injection Attacks on Jev's Typed Probabilistic Decisions
authors: Tiantong Wu; Wei Yang Bryan Lim
main_finding: Injected content raised the attacker-target probability by 0.043 on average but selected the target in only 1.8% of cases; adaptive search with score feedback doubled the best attacker probability (0.043 → 0.084) and raised validated success to 3.5%.
caveats: One proprietary version; three-choice primary space.; Measures selection, not harmful execution.; Success concentrates in cases with small initial decision margins.

title: Harness Tokenomics: A Router for the Enterprise Agentic Control Plane
authors: Ted Kwartler; Alan Aqrawi; Arian Abbasi
main_finding: In the emulation the router recovered 13–21% of model spend ($3.3M–5.1M a year for 10,000 seats); Jev answered each classification in about 250 ms median from a laptop.
caveats: Synthetic scenarios written by the authors; savings are emulated, not measured in deployment.; One vendor’s list prices.; Routing quality is assumed from cache and payback rules, not validated against outcomes.

title: Calibrated Decision Models for Autonomous Penetration-Testing Harnesses: JEV and Laya as System One Decision Layers for LLM-Driven Pentest Agents
authors: Joas Antonio dos Santos Barbosa
main_finding: In one run each, the Jev-enabled harness finished 5 min 19 s faster and graded severity differently (8 High vs 3); the author states these observations motivate the design but are not a controlled experiment.
caveats: Single run per arm; no statistical comparison.; Most performance figures are quoted from other papers or projections.; Single author.

title: From Text Decisions to Pixels: An Study of Jev-Style Visual Choice Model
authors: Xunlan Zhou; Xianliang Yang; Li Zhao
main_finding: 64-shot source adaptation raised Pets accuracy from 60.13% to 92.40% and transferred to new labels and A-OKVQA; a matched prompt-only control rose by the same amount (56.36% → 91.63%), so the gain came from adaptation rather than from the typed readout. A DINOv2 probe remained ahead on the source tasks.
caveats: Small open checkpoints (2B, 4B); no hosted model.; Specialist probes still lead on recognition.; No released code located.

title: Just Ask Jev: Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions as a Zero-Shot Detector of AI Alignment Failures
authors: Ruoqi Guo; Yi Liu; Gelei Deng; Yuekang Li; Lida Zhao; Yutao Wu; Simin Chen; Ying Zhang; Leo Yu Zhang
main_finding: A generic yes/no question ranked most failures well (median AUROC 0.886 over 31 benchmarks) at about 1/63 of the judges’ cost, but probabilities did not transfer as thresholds (median ECE 0.168 against a null of 0.074); supplying the reference that defines a failure gave the large gains.
caveats: Many failures are relational: the detector must be given the defining reference.; Labels are mostly benchmark-judge labels; two benchmarks have human labels.; Small target models.

title: JEV vs. LLMs as Rubric Judges: Cheaper, Faster, and Wrong in the Same Places
authors: Delip Rao; Chris Callison-Burch
main_finding: Jev’s accuracy differed significantly from the LLM judges in only 8 of 27 paired comparisons (ahead mostly on binary criteria, behind only on ordinal ones) while the judges cost 16–325 times as much and took 28–350 times as long; the judges repeated 96% of Jev’s most confident errors, so cascades gained at most 2.7 points even with oracle thresholds.
caveats: Observational: expectations formed on binary panels and tested on ordinal ones.; Ordinal labels follow unstated rating conventions that all judges miss.; Flash-tier judges only.

title: Jev-Mobile: Jev as an Executor for Mobile GUI Agents
authors: Linghua Zhang
main_finding: Jev-Mobile completed 79% of AndroidWorld tasks (SeeAct-V 78%, step-wise VLM 84%) and, on successful trajectories, cut mean time by 32.7% and model API cost by 73.4% against the step-wise VLM.
caveats: AndroidWorld only; not tested on web interfaces.; Jev was not swapped for another executor in the same workflow.; Single author; no version or code stated.

title: Jev in the Wild: A Data-Driven Analysis of the Jev Model's Functionality, Applications and Ecosystem
authors: Guoming Ling; Muen Xue; Zijian Ye
main_finding: Use is spread across domains (no category above 18% of projects); attribute judgment (77%) and scoring (52%) are the most common purposes, 69.7% of projects use Jev for two or more purposes, and routing and automation projects receive 41.4% of all stars.
caveats: Snapshot of one week; public GitHub only.; Labels assigned by an LLM agent with a second LLM review.; Stars measure attention, not use or quality.

title: JevOut: Natural Context Can Flip Decision Models
authors: Zixiang Xu
main_finding: Within 64 accepted target evaluations, optimised context redirected 312 of 508 initially correct Jev decisions (61.4%), with 229 reaching at least 0.7 probability on the wrong target; a single target-aware addition flipped 16.9% against 2.2% for a neutral addition.
caveats: Additions are optimised with probability feedback.; Fluency judged by a model, not by people.; One hosted version.

title: Auditing System-1 Models on Biosecurity-Relevant Benchmarks: Calibration, Selective Prediction, and Permutation Instability in a Non-Generative Model
authors: Kimon Antonios Provatas; Ilias Georgakopoulos-Soares
main_finding: Read correctly, the confidence field is calibrated overall (pooled ECE 0.034, AUROC 0.820) and deferring the least confident 40% raised WMDP-Bio accuracy from 85.2% to 97.1%; but four cyclic option rotations changed the answer on 37.4% of WMDP-Cyber items, 28.2 points beyond run-to-run variation.
caveats: WMDP accuracy is a proxy for hazardous knowledge, not a capability claim.; Per-task calibration varies widely (ECE 0.033–0.193).; One hosted version.

title: LAVOIR: Teaching a Single-Pass Decision Encoder When and What to Ask with Amortized Value of Information
authors: Furkan Yilmaz; Habibe Aleyna Tasdemir; Muhammed Faruk Gozay
main_finding: With group temperatures, the learned policy reached an accuracy–questions AUC of 0.799–0.800 against 0.800–0.803 for the oracle, with 88–92% top-1 agreement on which slot to ask about; zero-shot decisions stayed 15 points below the Bayes ceiling.
caveats: Synthetic dialogues from a simulator; real-data tests cover single exchanges.; Laya and Jev comparison figures are taken from other reports.

title: JevSoup: System-One Routing for Training-Free LoRA Composition
authors: Xiuying Wang; Jiahua Cheng; Shuotian Li; Yufan Cheng; Bowen Deng; Zhexuan Bai; Yichen Li
main_finding: JevSoup exceeded the strongest external baseline by up to 1.19 points in task-macro accuracy; routing with Jev Top-2 beat Jev Top-1 by 1.40 macro points.
caveats: Five-page workshop paper; small margins on one benchmark.; Gains mix routing and orthogonal composition.

title: JevAdvBench: A Benchmark and Black-Box Attacks for Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions Models
authors: Jianyi Hu; Hangtao Zhang; Yi Liu; Yeqi Zeng; Li Zeng; Xianlong Wang; Rui Wang; Leo Yu Zhang
main_finding: An observer’s opinion appended to the state flipped 12.1% of decisions, tied with the strongest injected command (10.1%), and pushed 38.0% of confident answers below a 0.8 confidence gate (0.5% under a re-run); benign paraphrase stayed within 1.2 points of the 1.0% noise floor. An identical re-run changed the Score value on 38.5% of Score questions.
caveats: 82.4% of labels are the model’s own consensus answers, so flips rather than accuracy are the measure.; One hosted version; vendor reference questions make up part of the set.

title: Beyond Calibration: Do a Typed-Decision Model's Probabilities Obey the Probability Axioms?
authors: Keyi Li; Yihao He; Quanyi Li
main_finding: Jev’s probabilities for “the label is X” and “the label is not X” missed summing to one by 0.064 on average (Qwen3.8-27B: 0.293 first-token, 0.122 verbalised); Jev was still incoherent — violations about five times its repeat noise, and its three single-label probabilities summed to 1.14 on average.
caveats: Small by design: 160 items, two English domains, one wording each.; Label-free checks show inconsistency, not which answer is right.

title: Evaluating System One Models for Agent Security Decisions: Reliability, Calibration, and Selective Automation
authors: Yixuan Liu
main_finding: Jev had a lower false-alarm rate than GPT-4.1 on WAInjectBench and an R-Judge AUROC of 0.961 against Laya’s 0.533, but under a fixed symmetric policy it could automate only 7.63% of R-Judge inputs within the error limits (47.03% with separately chosen block and allow thresholds); high average accuracy and low calibration error hid attacks scored safe with high confidence in particular groups.
caveats: Benchmarks differ in label construction; group-level failures need group-level tests.; Thresholds chosen on development data did not always transfer.

title: Jev Matches 7B Language Models for Speech-Neuroprosthesis Rescoring
authors: Gabriele Cinà
main_finding: Jev reached 7.5% word error against 7.8% for both 7B models (6.9% vs 7.2% and 7.4% with the decoder weight re-tuned), at $0.07 per thousand sentences and without a GPU; general LLMs asked to pick a sentence answered from list position.
caveats: One participant and one decoder.; Closed model: the result shows that a typed decision model can do the job, not why.; Internet latency (262 ms end to end) is not faster than a local 7B model (27 ms).

title: COGNIT-Guard: Calibrated Standalone Direct-Decision Guardrails with Heterogeneous CPU-NPU Confidence Cascading under Explicit Latency and False-Positive Constraints
authors: Hao Chen
main_finding: After supervised boundary adaptation the cascade reached 98.85% accuracy, 0.42% benign false-positive rate and 1.12% ECE on DUCS-Bench (zero-shot Laya ROC-AUC 0.827 vs 0.997 adapted), but in-domain adaptation cost out-of-distribution accuracy (60.33% → 56.81%), partly recovered with replay.
caveats: Single author; one in-house benchmark for the main result.; Zero-shot Laya is far weaker than the adapted model.

title: Type-Safe Decision Frameworks for Agentic 5G Control: A Theory-Driven Testbed Characterization of Where They Can Be Applied
authors: Michail-Alexandros Kourtis; George Xilouris
main_finding: Jev read new, runtime-declared questions without labels (≥0.98 on six of eight counterfactual templates) but reached only 0.67 on rule-defined known classes against 0.90–0.92 for fine-tuned specialists, and its network-bound latency (warm p50 281 ms, cold 726 ms) never met the 100 ms near-real-time classes.
caveats: Single testbed; real-time factor scaling of RAN timing.; Data leave the operator’s domain with a hosted model.

title: Laya as a Typed Probabilistic Assessor: An Independent Reproduction and a Preregistered Study of Calibration and Selective Escalation
authors: Gowthamkumar Nandakishore
main_finding: The reproduction matched the card’s accuracy (0.767 vs 0.766) but found the checkpoint uniformly under-confident (signed gap −0.214, every reliability bin below its accuracy), the opposite of the card’s warning; one temperature (T = 0.469) cut held-out ECE from 0.204 to 0.037, and the escalation gate missed its 10% error target.
caveats: Single checkpoint; benchmark labels come from a synthetic 4B-class teacher whose self-agreement (0.735) the model exceeds.; No zero-shot transfer out of distribution (accuracy 0.617).

title: JET: Justification Evaluation in Transformer
authors: Shenghao Ding
main_finding: The best local configuration reached 85.09% on full MMLU at 2.21 requests/s, 3.97 points below the author’s evaluation of Jev 1.13 (89.06% at 2.86 requests/s); prefix reuse and cache management gave 2.18–2.23× speedups with unchanged outputs.
caveats: Jev figure from a separate manual evaluation, not the same harness.; LoRA gain cannot be fully attributed (reference model from a separate conversion).; Single author.

title: Do System One Decisions Add Up? A Study of Probabilistic Coherence
authors: Saman Sarker Joy
main_finding: Both systems disagreed with themselves across granularities (mean category-level total variation 0.219–0.349 for Jev, 0.424–0.689 for Laya); reconstructing through categories cut Jev’s CLINC150 accuracy by 22.9 points but raised Laya’s by 21.3.
caveats: Exploratory; scope narrowed after pilots.; Instructions, choices, ordering and calibration change together.; Three English closed-set datasets.

title: Jev in Medicine: A Benchmark Evaluation
authors: Alfredo Madrid-García; Beatriz Merino-Barbancho
main_finding: Jev matched GPT-6 Sol on PubMedQA (78.4% vs 78.2%) but trailed on MetaMedQA (74.8% vs 82.7%) and far behind on DiagnosisArena-MCQ (59.8% vs 82.4%) and NEJM cases (61.8% vs 82.4%); it chose “I don’t know” on only 10.5% of 162 unanswerable questions. All 2,823 items cost US$0.08.
caveats: Text-only: images replaced by captions.; Reference answers used as published.; One version; no clinical validation.

title: Decision Readouts for Text-Mediated Video Anomaly Detection: An Exploratory Evaluation of Jev and Qwen
authors: Xukui Qin; Youting Wang; Xinjie He; Ziyang Luo; Runxiong Wu; Yan-Syuan Chen; Zhongyao Chu
main_finding: On XD captions, Jev Noul reached 75.99% average precision against 48.47% for Qwen generated probability and 57.81% for the ordinal-likelihood readout (+18.18 points, 95% interval 5.53–31.50); UCF showed no corresponding advantage, and Jev Choice returned only 776 of 800 valid numerical answers.
caveats: Sparse development sample with few positives (10 and 37).; Text-mediated: depends on captioning quality.; Dataset-conditional result.

title: When Does Selection Replace Extraction? A Pre-Registered Test of Agent Memory with a Typed Decision Model
authors: Rishabh Sharma; Rishika Lall
main_finding: At a tight budget, raw turns selected by Jev were non-inferior to an LLM-extraction memory (one-sided 95% bound −3.0 against a −5-point margin) and cost 3,061 times less to write; the reranking gain shrank from +17.4 to +1.5 points as the budget grew.
caveats: One benchmark family per setting; LoCoMo dialogues are LLM-generated.; Extraction baseline not run on LongMemEval.

title: SeLMRoute: Probabilistic Semantic Evidence for Large Language Model Routing
authors: Vasilis Perifanis; Nikolaos Pavlidis; Symeon Symeonidis
main_finding: SeLMRoute reached 72.08% average accuracy against 69.23% for the strongest single model; the 40-dimensional probability state beat 88 hard features, dense embeddings and TF-IDF, and the JEV-based state outperformed the Laya-based one.
caveats: Single benchmark framework; published routers use a different split.; Requires a decision-model call per query.

title: JEV as a Judge for Agent Trace Security: An Empirical Comparison with Generative LLM Judges
authors: Zhiqiang Wang; Yichao Gao
main_finding: JEV reached a benchmark-averaged positive-class F1 of 77.8 against 74.1 for the strongest generative judge (GLM-5.2), leading on ATBench500 and MCPHunt but trailing on R-Judge and TraceSafe, at 0.99 s median latency and about $0.000195 per judgment.
caveats: Common threshold; performance varies by dataset.; Valid-result coverage 95.5%.; No version or code stated.

title: JevVibe: Efficient Classification-Guided Secure Code Generation
authors: Arshak Rezvani; Sasha Behrouzi; Ahmad-Reza Sadeghi
main_finding: Jev beat all six open models (Top-1 0.458 vs 0.335 for Qwen2.5-Coder-32B) but trailed GPT-5.6-Sol on Top-1 (0.495) while leading on Top-3/Top-5, at $0.283 against $15.83 and 0.244 s against 1.531 s median latency; Jev-guided repair raised the security pass rate from 63.5% to 70.7% (LLM-guided 66.1%).
caveats: One benchmark; detector-based pass rate.; Top-1 below the frontier model.

title: NavJev: Efficient Vision-Language Navigation via Action-Centric Visual Compression and Discriminative Action-Semantic Memory
authors: Kai Sheng; Liuyi Wang; Jinlong Li; Haojie Dai; Chengju Liu; Qijun Chen
main_finding: NavJev reached 27.0% success and 22.4% SPL at 0.65 s per step, 41.5× faster than Open-Nav (which reached 19.0% SR with GPT-4o); used as the decision layer, Jev beat Qwen3.8-Max and GPT-4o by 2.0 and 13.0 SR points at 0.53 s per decision.
caveats: Low absolute success; compression components carry much of the gain (SR 19 → 27 in the ablation).; Text-only decisions depend on captioners.

title: The Argument and the Letterhead: Source-Position Coherence in AI Evaluation
authors: Michele Loi
main_finding: Source–argument interactions appeared across chat models; the Jev supplement (288 ratings) also showed five interactions above the adopted 0.05 reference, though its distinct rubric and interrupted collection limit comparison.
caveats: Descriptive studies; the Jev supplement uses a different rubric.; Small number of fixed texts.

title: Decide, Don't Generate: Competitive Dimensional ABSA with Jev's Typed Decisions
authors: Yiqun Zhang; Peidong Wang; Zihan Wang; Shi Feng
main_finding: The system reached 1.0645 RMSE on valence–arousal regression, the lowest aggregate error of any participating system, and 52.09 / 44.06 continuous F1 on triplet and quadruplet extraction, above fine-tuned 70B and 120B baselines; supervised calibration roughly halved the raw regression error.
caveats: Uses labelled data for 488 fitted coefficients.; Extraction errors remain structural (span proposal and selection).

title: Jev thinks "I don't know'', but doesn't say it: Introducing Sys1Cal-v1 Dataset for Probability Calibration
authors: Riccardo Porcedda
main_finding: Noul and Score answers were close to the true probabilities (soft accuracy 0.918 and 0.886) but Choice answers were not (0.764; SemIf 0.629); estimating an implicit “unknown” component lifted Choice to 0.931.
caveats: Synthetic; isolates probability semantics rather than broad competence.; Single author; Score needs a projection to True/False.

title: PACT: Pairwise-Anchored Calibrated Tuning for Single-Token Typed Decisions
authors: Yida Lin
main_finding: PACT did not beat the properly reproduced Nimble recipe on accuracy (84.6% vs 85.2%) or calibration, but it had the lowest position bias (answer flips under relabelling 9.8% vs 13.8%) and ordinal error, and against a cross-entropy control it halved seed-to-seed spread and cut NLL by 26%.
caveats: No single term raises raw accuracy; gains are in robustness and stability.; One curated dataset and backbone.

title: Mnemon: Raw Records, Fast Judgments, Slow Thoughts
authors: Guangren Wang
main_finding: Mnemon reached 91.7% on LoCoMo and 83.8% on LongMemEval-S from under 4k tokens of context per question (92.2% and 94.4% with a reasoning model as System 2); on the same records Jev separated gold evidence better than two LLMs (AUC 0.942 vs 0.900 and 0.853) at 3–11 times their speed.
caveats: No held-out benchmark: developed on the evaluation sets.; LLM graders; different graders from the comparison systems.

title: Koa-action: Fast and Consistent Structured Decision Making with Generative LLMs
authors: Shenghong Dai; Shiva Kumar Pentyala; Yingchi Liu; Shubham Mehrotra; Suman Banerjee; James Zhu; Bin Bi; Sitaram Asur; Phil Mui
main_finding: Koa-action reached 85.5% on intent routing, within 2 points of the strongest frontier models, at 0.53 s median (1.9–7.5× faster) with a flat tail across label-space sizes; the authors report it competitive with Jev on accuracy and faster at the median.
caveats: Industrial benchmark not public.; Jev comparison reported qualitatively in the abstract.

title: Dyad: Extending Large Language Models with Native Typed Decision-Making
authors: Yundaichuan Zhan; Weishi Wang; Wenbiao Liu; Daniel Dahlmeier; Chengwei Qin; Juncheng Li; Fredrik D. Johansson; Zhongqi Yue
main_finding: With the LLM frozen, training only the action encoder gave consistent gains on four unseen environments (up to 5.89 points on ALFWorld with GRPO); on JevBench, Dyad with reasoning reached 86.18% against Jev’s 85.01%.
caveats: Training pipeline not yet released.; JevBench comparison mixes reasoning and non-reasoning settings.

title: More Features Are Not More Evidence: Limits of Training-Free Human Activity Recognition with Jev
authors: Orhan Konak
main_finding: Jev stayed far below supervised recognition (best macro-F1 0.038, 0.118 and 0.089 across the three datasets); a semantic rendering of the numbers partly helped, and its probabilities were not reliably calibrated for recognition.
caveats: Representation and semantics change together.; Post-hoc fusion analysis did not replicate.

title: Calibrated to Whom? Persona and Language Effects on Cultural Values in JEV
authors: Bushra Asseri; Abdulaziz Asseri
main_finding: Answers were highly repeatable (ICC 0.997); without a persona they resembled Jev’s own American personas, and switching to Saudi personas reproduced 87% of the human Saudi–US difference in English but 62% in Arabic, with long-term orientation reversed.
caveats: One model version; one Arabic translation.; Hofstede scores from unmatched samples and periods.

title: Chinese-Jev: Bringing System One Model to Chinese-Language Tasks
authors: Zexiao Wang; Zihao Zhang; Xudong Wang; Pan Wang; Ziyi Ye; Haoyu Zhao; Zuxuan Wu; Shuicheng Yan
main_finding: After pre-training, Chinese-Jev reached 69.20% on the general subset, slightly above hosted Jev (1.24% relative), and cut ECE from 11.45% to 3.78%; after domain fine-tuning it reached 92% of Jev’s average accuracy across three specialised domains at about 15 ms per decision.
caveats: Benchmark built by the authors.; No released weights or code located.

title: Probability Contracts: Accuracy, Coherence, and Decisions Across LLM Interfaces
authors: Han Chen; Yingrui Li
main_finding: Kev had lower aggregate posterior error than Jev but larger complement and coarsening residuals; Jev’s Event and Choice interfaces chose different binary actions on 32.8% of valid pairs at a deferral cost of 0.10, and interface disagreement certified only 11–52% of the actual error.
caveats: Synthetic worlds with exact posteriors.; Two systems and four interfaces.

title: Evaluating and Benchmarking the System One Model Jev
authors: Tobias Deußer; Lorenz Sparrenberg; Rafet Sifa
main_finding: Jev beat Qwen3.8-27B on 27 of 37 datasets (none of Qwen’s nine leads outside the intervals) and Gemma on all 37, with pooled Choice ECE 0.028; binary probabilities ranked well but sat poorly against a fixed 0.5 threshold (tuned thresholds raised UNFAIR-ToS micro-F1 from 0.50 to 0.75). Rotating options left accuracy unchanged, and calculation-heavy MMLU questions were easier for Jev than other MMLU questions (94% vs 91%).
caveats: One untuned template per dataset.; MMLU result may reflect memorised question–answer pairs.; All models degrade on low-resource languages and rubric judgments.

title: Can a Cacheable Decision Model Follow Rules?
authors: Dushyant Rajput; Nirdesh Chauhan; Siddharth Kosaraju
main_finding: Converting to cacheable scoring cut rule-sensitive recall@1 from 1.00 to 0.24 while the joint scorer held 1.00 (about 5× more expensive at 77 candidates); counterfactual supervision restored held-out synthetic rule tasks, but on real rules the joint scorer kept its edge (0.861 vs 0.500 on the short tier).
caveats: Real-rule evaluations are small (tens of items per slice).; Paper does not compare with hosted Jev.

title: More Choices, Fewer Decisions: Ordinal-Scale Bias in JEV-like Direct-Decision Models
authors: Tianxiang Gao; Jinzhe Li; Zhiyuan Li; Yi Chang; Yuan Wu
main_finding: Jev reached 74.95% on ANLI yet assigned 38.8% of all predictions and 51.3% of its errors to Neutral, regardless of candidate position; across 36 ordinal datasets decisions used only 67–76% of effective gold support against 87–102% on nominal tasks, and utilisation fell as scales were refined from 2 to 14 levels.
caveats: Ordinal/nominal split is a binary taxonomy.; Same-item scaling covers three ordinal sources.

title: OpenJev-RLCD: A Working RLCD Implementation
authors: Zhimin Gao; Pichao Wang
main_finding: With Qwen3-1.7B on two reasoning tasks, RLCD matched or beat SFT, RFT/STaR and GRPO in accuracy and beat all of them in selective prediction; when uncertainty comes from annotator disagreement, RLCD provably cannot beat cross-entropy.
caveats: 1.7B model, 400–800 steps, three seeds.; GSM8K-Verify built by the authors.

title: Bongard: Training Machine Intuition
authors: Li Ding; Haidi Jin; Chen Ji
main_finding: Joint-embedding post-training raised held-out rephrasing accuracy from 75.7% to 85.9% and the sandbox stage raised a frozen sandbox panel from 50.6% to 64.8%; the final model reached 78.05% on DecisionBench (fourth of 61 systems in the public comparison) with 36 ms median latency for short requests and 221 ms for 32 questions about one state on one RTX PRO 6000.
caveats: Leaderboard rank is a snapshot of a community benchmark.; The alignment stage is isolated only by a short control.; Weights under the Gemma terms of use, not an OSI licence.

title: When the Right Answer Is Missing: An Arithmetic-Dependent Rejection Bottleneck in Jev
authors: Jike Zhong; Ming Li; Yuxiang Lai
main_finding: Answer-present accuracy reached 99% while correct rejection fell to 7%, a gap that persisted across magnitudes, depths, contexts and rejection labels; Boolean verification of the same candidates correctly rejected 99% of answer-absent cases, and a threshold chosen on separate development problems raised rejection to 79% while keeping 97% answer-present accuracy.
caveats: Hosted API only; mechanisms are inferred from inputs and outputs.; Synthetic arithmetic tasks.

title: Decision-Oriented Recommendation Reranking: An Empirical Study of Jev
authors: Hanjia Lyu; Yinglong Xia
main_finding: Jev generally achieved the highest NDCG@10 on Video Games and Books and stayed strong as candidate sets grew, while its observed latency grew far more gradually than pointwise Qwen reranking but stayed well above SASRec and DCNv2.
caveats: Results reported mainly in figures.; Hosted latency includes network and gateway overhead; local baselines do not.; One decision model; larger LLM rerankers not tested.

title: Counting the Uncounted: Population-Level Surveillance of Documented Pregnancy and Fetal Harm in Police Crash Narratives with a System One Model (Jev)
authors: Amir Rafe; Subasish Das
main_finding: Jev confirmed 5,333 narratives documenting a pregnant person; blind adjudication of a probability-stratified sample gave weighted sensitivity 0.999 and specificity 1.000, yielding an estimated 5,467 crashes with a documented pregnancy (95% interval 5,306–5,577), including 58 documenting fetal harm.
caveats: Narratives under a data agreement; not public.; Documentation is not occurrence: narratives record 2.56–3.09% of expected pregnant drivers.

title: Benchmarking System One decision models against trained classifiers and language models for automated decision gates
authors: Amir Rafe; Subasish Das
main_finding: The ranking of model classes depended on conditions: trained classifiers led on intents when labels existed, while most decision models beat zero-shot entailment without labels; a held-out threshold for 5% in-scope risk still let Jev accept 0.310 of out-of-scope requests, swapping yes and no flipped 50.5 of every 100 Jev answers, and an intent-trained first stage escalating to Jev matched its accuracy at 0.43 of its cost.
caveats: Same author team as other studies in this family.; Cost ratio assumes full GPU utilisation.; No code release located.

title: A First Glance at Jev for Network Traffic Classification: Accuracy, Processing Time, and Cost
authors: Shenghe Xu; Lifan Mei
main_finding: Zero-shot Jev reached 9.80% accuracy, below the 22.79% majority constant; 40 labelled examples raised it to 28.42% and 150 examples to 34.50% on the first test week, while tree ensembles trained on 8,000 records reached 69.95% and 66.80% and beat Jev in every week.
caveats: Unequal supervision budgets between Jev and the trees.; Fixed service configurations; raw responses not released.

title: OmniMed-Jev: Calibrating LVLM Confidence for Trustworthy Medical Multimodal Decisions via System One
authors: Luyao Tang; Cheng Chen
main_finding: The decision-native model’s probabilities tracked correctness far more closely, cutting calibration error by up to an order of magnitude and reliability error by up to two orders, while point predictions stayed comparable; counting was the one family where the generative baseline stayed ahead.
caveats: Interface and associated training differences cannot be separated.; Retrospective benchmarks; not evidence of clinical readiness.

title: JevSpawn: Adaptive Agentic Inference through Compositional Action Spaces
authors: Haoyang Su; Weiran Huang
main_finding: JevSpawn reached success rates of 0.96 and 0.95 on Maze and Grid (FoldAgent 0.52 and 0.73) and cut end-to-end latency there from 47.91 and 61.44 s to about 41 s; inside the same architecture hosted Jev beat Qwen scoring on three tasks, matched one and trailed on four, and took 1.4–2.1 times as long including API communication.
caveats: Puzzle environments.; Hosted variant timing includes network communication.

title: AnyJev Technical Report
authors: Jiamu Zhang; Tianze Yang; Yucheng Shi; Evan Chen; Zixiang Nie; Kelly Wan; Liangjie Hong; Ninghao Liu; Liang Wu
main_finding: Reversing the option list changed the answer on about 33% of items averaged over eleven models; rotation averaging lowered the order-flip rate on two 20-option tasks from 0.33 to 0.14 and 0.18 and raised accuracy for 11 of 11 models on both, and the stopping rule served 2.2 times as many decisions per second on vLLM.
caveats: One prefill cannot reason: hardest JevBench tier spans 0.343–0.590.; JevBench items average 3.6 options, where rotation helps least.

title: Beyond Answer Confidence: A Controlled Audit of Self-Knowledge in a Black-Box Decision Model
authors: Sharath M Shankaranarayana; Davor Runje; Jan Jannink
main_finding: Jev was calibrated on familiar closed-choice tasks but its confidence failed as a missing-knowledge signal: with no answer-relevant information it put up to 0.80 on a salient option, and on news beyond its knowledge boundary confidence exceeded accuracy by 0.21–0.33 even after recalibration on earlier months; targeted yes/no questions on whether an outcome is settled (AUROC 1.00) or evidence suffices (0.95 vs 0.85) worked better, while “do you know?” questions mostly tracked surface cues.
caveats: One version of one closed model.; Follow-up questions evaluated on curated contrasts.

title: Jev-IDS: System One Models for Network Intrusion Detection
authors: Paulo Severo; Silvio E. Quincozes; Amanda Dias
main_finding: At one example per category Jev was 4.8 times faster and 3.8 times cheaper than GPT-5.6 Luna with 1.5 times higher novel-attack recall, and raised 15 times fewer false alarms than the low-data Random Forest; across 5,400 decisions it reached F1 0.859 (precision 0.941, recall 0.790), and two examples lowered F1 to 0.839.
caveats: 300-flow pilot on a historical dataset.; Low-data Random Forest is a weak reference.

title: Permutation-Robust Decision Modeling with Candidate-Independent Block-Causal Attention
authors: Guy Amit
main_finding: Candidate isolation cut test permutation flip rates from 8.3% to 0.1% (Gemma 3 1B), 18.2% to 1.2% (Qwen3 1.7B) and 7.2% to 0.7% (Qwen3 4B) while keeping competitive accuracy (84.96% vs 81.84% on Qwen3 1.7B); isolation was the main source of the effect and position resetting completed it.
caveats: Single author; open backbones up to 4B.; Dual-encoder comparison not optimisation-matched.

title: Code Owns the Simulation, Jev Owns the Evaluation
authors: Yaodong Yang; Hongyao Tang; Yi Ma; Xingyu Fan; Weixun Wang; Jinpeng Li; Tianpei Yang
main_finding: Jev answered 99% of Cognitive Reflection Test questions correctly but played games as if a rational opponent moved at random; stating the opponent’s action raised accuracy from 33% to 98%, a two-call decomposition reached 94%, and a code lookahead raised ALFWorld games solved from 31% to 87%.
caveats: Single model version; hand-built decompositions.; No code release located.

title: Prune First, Decide Fast: Scalable Semantic Query Processing with JEVDB
authors: Zhengle Wang; Hanxu Yan; Fuheng Zhao; Chunwei Liu
main_finding: On SemBench the Flash configuration had the lowest latency on all 21 queries and the lowest cost on 19 with competitive quality; on Shelob it completed every query with 95.7–97.5% mean F1 where baselines timed out, Semantic Bloom Filters removed 87.4% of candidate pairs before evaluation and reusable condition scoring cut escalations by 55.2%.
caveats: Authors’ own benchmark for joins.; Gains combine pruning, batching and the decision model.

title: HydroJEV: A one-second, training-free screen for cyber-attack and fault attribution in water distribution networks
authors: Tianwei Mu; Shengyan Jiang; Mingzhe Yuan; Qing Luo; Min Xiao; Wenhong Wang; Jun Li; Manhong Huang
main_finding: With only a label-free prior correction, Jev matched the rule tree in distribution (macro-F1 0.62–0.64 vs 0.56–0.61), beat the supervised classifier by 0.36–0.42 on event subtypes absent from its labels in all four rounds, and decided 20–40 times faster than frontier LLMs; accepting only benign Jev verdicts confirmed by the rule tree spared an LLM reviewer 35–38% of windows without loss of macro-F1.
caveats: All windows simulated with one hydraulic model.; LLM timings from one client at one time.

title: LLM-as-Jev: LLMs Are Already Jev-Style Decision Models -- When and How to Fine-Tune Them
authors: Yinheng Li; Justin Wagle
main_finding: Frozen Qwen3.5-4B resolved 188 of 231 public JevBench items (81.4%), matching community models built on the same backbone, handled all 77 Banking77 intents in one pass (69.0%) and reached 82.4% on MMBench with images; fine-tuning helped the 0.6B model and many-option routing most, and LoRA with KL anchors gave the best 4B model (84.0%, ECE 0.050).
caveats: Public JevBench items only (231).; Two backbones from one family.

title: Fast Models, Slow Evidence: A Paired and Self-Audited Evaluation of System-1 Decision Models for LLM Agent Harnesses
authors: Jiawei Li
main_finding: Jev was significantly more accurate on 9 of 11 decision points (+10.8 to +46.0 pp); neither beat chance on zero-shot model routing and they tied on RAG relevance gating. Laya changed 30% of answers when options were reversed and fell to 31% with 50 near-duplicate tools against 98% for Jev. The self-audit found that an omitted pre-screen cost turned a reported 23.9% saving into 4.3%, gate accuracy had been reported as end-to-end quality (58% vs 98%), and in-sample thresholds aimed at 5% misses gave up to 17% on held-out data.
caveats: Single versions, zero-shot, English-dominant public data.; About 5 pp wording band on absolute accuracies.

title: HakemBench: A Turkish Benchmark of Typed Decisions
authors: Sait Furkan Teke
main_finding: Three hosted chat models and Jev 1.13 led the 16-row board (composites 0.825–0.888); Jev ranked fourth at 0.825 with a median of 135 ms against 1,294 ms for the leader. The lab’s own model ranked seventh (0.660), and its numbers are not blind because earlier test results shaped its training data.
caveats: Gold labels mostly AI-made and not human-verified; one human annotator.; The benchmark’s authors also build a ranked model.

title: From Retrieval to Typed Decisions: Calibrated System One Models from Biomedical Sentence Encoders
authors: Pritam Deka
main_finding: Retrieval training helped zero-shot matching and helped the PFR head in 10 of 15 fine-tuned comparisons but helped the cross head in one and hurt it in five; the cross head beat PFR under every objective, and the released RLCD recipe trailed cross-entropy by 2.5–3.0 points because its reward normalisation inflated a noisy gradient term 3.6–15-fold.
caveats: Base-size encoders and one training budget.; Parent–retriever pairs share parents; not independent replications.

title: Labels Override Definitions in Jev-Style Typed Decision Models
authors: Seyedarmin Azizi; Erfan Baghaei Potraghloo; Massoud Pedram
main_finding: Deleting every definition left laya-td accuracy unchanged (0.8559 vs 0.8487) although definitions alone supported 0.7971, and renaming options to A and B raised routing accuracy by 0.151; rendering options without the label made all three laya checkpoints exactly invariant, while adding labels created the effect in von, whose accuracy fell from 0.8511 to 0.2281 when a label contradicted its definition.
caveats: Hosted Jev not measured.; PolicyBench is synthetic and templated.

title: SecJev: Bringing Security Expertise to System One Decision Models
authors: Zheng Chen; Fei Yu; Haohao Huang; Yang Li; Anlong Chen; Lei Chen
main_finding: Security specialisation improved every model in the family: SecJev-0.8B gained 39.40 points of task-macro accuracy over Kev-0.8B and beat general Kev-9B by 20.51 points, with accuracy and latency close to answer-only generative fine-tuning at lower peak memory; gains over Kev held on new prompt-injection and traffic sources, with capture-dependent false alarms.
caveats: Tasks measure source-label prediction and displayed-rule application, not end-to-end defence.; Uneven task sizes.

title: To Jev or Not? Evaluating the Accuracy and Efficiency of Structured Decision Models for Hate-Speech Moderation
authors: Demetris Paschalides; George Pallis; Marios D. Dikaiakos
main_finding: Commercial LLMs significantly beat all decision models on only one of four datasets (by 4.1–5.9 macro-F1), and supervised classifiers lost up to 54 points out of distribution; supplying definitions changed up to 28% of predictions but improved agreement in only 29% of comparisons, decomposition helped in 20% and hurt in 37%, and the best hosted decision model came within 1.6 points of the best commercial LLM at about 97% lower inference cost.
caveats: Definitions differ across datasets.; No code release located.

title: Benchmarking Candidate Coverage in Typed Decision Models
authors: Jiawen Lu; Tongtong Wu
main_finding: Native rejection differed sharply: with five TREC candidates and natural names, Laya detected 97.2% of missing-answer cases but falsely rejected 69.7% of present controls, while Jev detected 24.8% and falsely rejected none; thresholds fitted on calibration pairs moved these to 33.9%/3.7% (Laya) and 45.0%/1.8% (Jev).
caveats: Small, roughly balanced samples; one replicate per candidate count.; Limited to reference-label omission; no out-of-scope generalisation claim.

title: General Decision Models: Benchmarking and Insights Beyond Jev
authors: Feiyu Duan; Jiayu Lin; Jia Wang; Jun Xiang; Jialiang Wu; Xinnong Zhang; Hanqi Yan; Siyuan Wang; Zhongyu Wei
main_finding: The strongest decision models came within three points of leading thinking LLMs overall but fell behind on specialist knowledge; Jev picked the mode on all 100 prior-probability items yet put 89.35% of the mass on it against 35.60% in the true distribution; in τ-bench, Jev action selection cut median episode time from 267 s to 161 s but lowered success from 77.6% to 66.1%; InnerJev-27B performed on par with Jev at about 0.1 s per query.
caveats: Two agentic settings only.; InnerJev is the authors’ own model.

title: System One Models for Wireless Decision-Making:Applications and Performance Evaluation
authors: Masoud Rahimi; S. M. Matin Alemohammad; Hamid Behroozi; Mahdi Nouri
main_finding: In receive-antenna selection Jev cut median response latency by up to 8.5 times against the evaluated LLMs but lost decision quality to stronger task-specific methods; in intent-conditioned RAN slicing it reached utility comparable to the LLMs with more than 3.5 times lower median latency. Faster decisions did not necessarily mean lower end-to-end service latency.
caveats: Client-observed latency of a hosted service.; Edge-orchestration evidence comes from an earlier study by other authors, not a new experiment.

title: Hidden Risks of Jev: An Empirical Study of Security, Privacy, and Dual Use
authors: Shang Wang; Tianqing Zhu; Huajie Chen; Jiayang Li; Meng Yang; Bo Liu
main_finding: Context-ignoring injection reached 96.5% attack success against Jev on support routing and Jev-specific injections reached 100% on subscription cancellation and at least 96.8% on issue severity; backdoors implanted by poisoning NanoJev succeeded on over 89% of targeted inputs while clean accuracy stayed at 90.5–94.0%; as a detector Jev reached ROC-AUC 0.95–1.0 on all eight benchmarks, and the same capability supported jailbreak planning and model extraction.
caveats: Backdoor and membership experiments use the open NanoJev, not the hosted model.; Application tasks constructed by the authors.

title: SearchJev: A Fast and Calibrated System-1 Model for Search Agents
authors: Congfeng Cao; Lipeng Zuo; Konstantinos Papakostas; Qiwei Xu; Songwei Xu; Lun Zhou; Zhaochun Ren; Yougang Lyu; Xiaohui Yan
main_finding: SearchJev beat same-size Qwen3.5 autoregressive models in decision quality while deciding 5.2–5.3 times faster with 41–74% lower average ECE; on held-out data it exceeded hosted Jev on query rewriting (and the 4B model on relevance) while Jev stayed stronger on routing and verification; in BrowseComp-Plus the dual-system agents cut median active search time 3.7–4.7-fold and raised answer accuracy from 45% to up to 54%.
caveats: Authors’ own benchmark.; Jev compared through its API on the same items.

title: GraphDecide: Benchmarking System One Models on Graph Tasks
authors: Xianliang Yang; Yapu Zhang; Li Zhao
main_finding: Jev answered every adjacency query correctly and did well on cycle, connectivity and distance, yet reached only 67.80% on exact degree and 61.25% on articulation points; joint graph-text input did not consistently improve prediction, and feasible constructions did not imply good solutions.
caveats: Small public instances; no claim for large or dynamic graphs.; Shares authors with PixelJev.

title: JEV versus LLMs: Accuracy, Cost and Calibration on Seven Political Science Replications
authors: Matthew DiGiuseppe; Steven Denney
main_finding: Jev matched or came close to both LLMs across tasks, but had no cost advantage over GPT-6 Luna at batch prices because it billed 1.2–3.3 times as many input tokens per decision; asked once, its probabilities were better calibrated than GPT-6 Luna’s token probabilities but not consistently better than Qwen3.8-27B’s.
caveats: Seven tasks from one discipline.; No code release located.

title: ufakzeka-karar: An Open Turkish Typed-Decision Model with Order-Invariant Option Scoring
authors: Sait Furkan Teke
main_finding: Scoring options blind to each other made answers independent of order by construction, while a sequential head trained on shuffled options changed 2.3–2.8% of answers when only the order changed; REINFORCE lost 0.102 macro-F1 to cross-entropy. The released model ranks 7th of 16 on HakemBench (composite 0.660) at a median of 102.5 ms on one CPU thread, and temperature scaling raised held-out calibration error (0.027 → 0.045).
caveats: Numbers are not blind: training data and the final run were shaped by reading test results.; Benchmark and model by the same author.; One human annotator.

title: Passage Re-ranking with BERT
authors: Rodrigo Nogueira; Kyunghyun Cho
main_finding: Cross-encoder reranking with BERT: a query–passage pair in, one relevance probability out — the template for scoring a supplied candidate without generating text.

title: Generative or Discriminative? Revisiting Text Classification in the Era of Transformers
authors: Siva Rajesh Kasa; Karan Gupta; Sumegh Roychowdhury; Ashutosh Kumar; Yaswanth Biruduraju; Santhosh Kumar Kasa; Nikhil Priyatam Pattisapu; Arindam Bhattacharya; Shailendra Agarwal; Vijay huddar
main_finding: Controlled comparison of autoregressive, masked-LM, diffusion and encoder classifiers over fixed label sets, covering sample efficiency, calibration and ordinality — the trade-offs typed decision models inherit.

title: Llama Guard: LLM-based Input-Output Safeguard for Human-AI Conversations
authors: Hakan Inan; Kartikeya Upasani; Jianfeng Chi; Rashi Rungta; Krithika Iyer; Yuning Mao; Michael Tontchev; Qing Hu; Brian Fuller; Davide Testuggine; Madian Khabsa
main_finding: Safety classification over a fixed taxonomy, read from the probability of a single safe/unsafe token: the guardrail pattern that typed yes/no questions are compared against.

title: Constitutional Classifiers: Defending against Universal Jailbreaks across Thousands of Hours of Red Teaming
authors: Mrinank Sharma; Meg Tong; Jesse Mu; Jerry Wei; Jorrit Kruthoff; Scott Goodfriend; Euan Ong; Alwin Peng; Raj Agarwal; Cem Anil; Amanda Askell; Nathan Bailey; Joe Benton; Emma Bluemke; Samuel R. main_finding: Input and output classifiers trained from a written constitution to gate a frontier model against universal jailbreaks: the deployed policy-gate role that typed binary questions are proposed for.

title: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback
authors: Long Ouyang; Jeff Wu; Xu Jiang; Diogo Almeida; Carroll L. Wainwright; Pamela Mishkin; Chong Zhang; Sandhini Agarwal; Katarina Slama; Alex Ray; John Schulman; Jacob Hilton; Fraser Kelton; Luke Miller; Maddie Simens; Amanda Askell; Peter Welinder; Paul Christiano; Jan Leike; Ryan Lowe
main_finding: Reward models that score a whole response with one scalar in a single pass, trained from human preferences: an early, widely deployed non-generative judgment head.

main_finding: Reports that the pre-trained model was well calibrated and that post-training reduced calibration — the observation that calibration-oriented decision training responds to.

title: Beyond Binary Rewards: Training LMs to Reason About Their Uncertainty
authors: Mehul Damani; Isha Puri; Stewart Slocum; Idan Shenfeld; Leshem Choshen; Yoon Kim; Jacob Andreas
main_finding: Reinforcement learning with a calibration (Brier) reward alongside correctness, so a reasoning model’s stated confidence is trained to be calibrated: a published precedent for proper-scoring rewards in RL training of language models.

title: Balancing Classification and Calibration Performance in Decision-Making LLMs via Calibration Aware Reinforcement Learning
authors: Duygu Nur Yaldiz; Evangelia Spiliopoulou; Zheng Qi; Siddharth Varia; Srikanth Doss; Nikolaos Pappas
main_finding: Shows that RL with verifiable rewards makes decision-making LLMs overconfident while supervised fine-tuning calibrates better, and proposes calibration-aware RL for decision tokens.

title: Large Language Diffusion Models
authors: Shen Nie; Fengqi Zhu; Zebin You; Xiaolu Zhang; Jingyang Ou; Jun Hu; Jun Zhou; Yankai Lin; Ji-Rong Wen; Chongxuan Li
main_finding: A masked diffusion language model that fills many positions in parallel: the reference point for diffusion readouts used by some open Jev-like projects.

title: Mercury: Ultra-Fast Language Models Based on Diffusion
authors: Inception Labs; Samar Khanna; Siddhant Kharbanda; Shufan Li; Harshit Varma; Eric Wang; Sawyer Birnbaum; Ziyang Luo; Yanis Miraoui; Akash Palrecha; Stefano Ermon; Aditya Grover; Volodymyr Kuleshov
main_finding: Commercial diffusion language models that predict many tokens in parallel, reported as up to ten times faster than speed-optimised frontier models: a reference for non-autoregressive speed claims.

title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
authors: Woosuk Kwon; Zhuohan Li; Siyuan Zhuang; Ying Sheng; Lianmin Zheng; Cody Hao Yu; Joseph E. Gonzalez; Hao Zhang; Ion Stoica
main_finding: PagedAttention and KV-cache sharing for LLM serving: explains why several questions over one shared state can cost little more than one, independently of the readout.

title: DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines
authors: Omar Khattab; Arnav Singhvi; Paridhi Maheshwari; Zhiyuan Zhang; Keshav Santhanam; Sri Vardhamanan; Saiful Haq; Ashutosh Sharma; Thomas T. Joshi; Hanna Moazam; Heather Miller; Matei Zaharia; Christopher Potts
main_finding: Declarative typed signatures compiled into prompts and self-improving pipelines: the programming-model alternative to a hosted typed-decision API.

title: Let Me Speak Freely? A Study on the Impact of Format Restrictions on Performance of Large Language Models
authors: Zhi Rui Tam; Cheng-Kuang Wu; Yi-Lin Tsai; Chieh-Yen Lin; Hung-yi Lee; Yun-Nung Chen
main_finding: Finds that format restrictions can lower LLM reasoning accuracy: typed outputs should be compared with unconstrained answers, not only with constrained decoding.

title: Thinking Fast and Slow in AI
authors: Grady Booch; Francesco Fabiano; Lior Horesh; Kiran Kate; Jon Lenchner; Nick Linck; Andrea Loreggia; Keerthiram Murugesan; Nicholas Mattei; Francesca Rossi; Biplav Srivastava
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence 2021, 35(17), 15042-15046
main_finding: A research agenda built on the fast/slow (System 1 / System 2) distinction from cognitive science, which the “System One” product category borrows.

title: GateDrain: Availability Attacks and Admission-Side Defense for Confidence-Gated Edge-Cloud Inference
authors: Zonghua Gu; Julian Singh-Smith; Junlin Liao; Di Liu
main_finding: Shows that confidence-gated edge–cloud inference opens an availability attack: bounded perturbations lower confidence and push requests into a shared cloud queue, degrading tail latency for everyone; proposes admission-side budgets.

title: Do Not Cut When Uncertain: Rejectable and Calibrated Decision Heads for VLA Policies in Robotic Harvesting
authors: Heng Zhang
main_finding: Adds a typed, rejectable and calibrated decision head to a frozen vision-language-action policy for robotic harvesting, arguing that the right to refuse — not model scale — restores reliability under occlusion.

title: Student-Guided Teacher Distillation for Efficient LLM Task Routing: Positioning Against Jev-Style System-1 Classifiers
authors: Haifeng Wu; Srinivasan Manoharan; Jian Wan; Fangbo Tu; Junhua Zhao; Xin Chen
main_finding: Distils a compact classifier that shortlists 60 task categories for a zero-shot NLI reranker, positioned as a documented alternative to System One classifiers whose training is undocumented.

title: Judgement in the Age of Jev: From Evaluation Scarcity to Evaluation Abundance
authors: Richard Hill
main_finding: Perspective essay proposing a conditional Jevons hypothesis for machine evaluation: much cheaper evaluation may raise its organisational use where demand is latent, while shared criteria and errors can scale mistakes.

title: Typed Decision Models: An Early Evidence Audit and Evaluation Checklist
authors: Lijuan Tang; Yuemeng Zheng
main_finding: An early evidence audit of 28 studies posted 19–24 September 2026, concluding that the typed readout has not yet shown an accuracy advantage over comparable label-probability readouts, that the clearest gains are latency and cost, and proposing a 14-item evaluation checklist.

title: SoK: Semantic Decision Engines in Network Control Loops
authors: Delong Li; Chen Li; Xu Wang; Haochen Gong; Rui Lang; Guangsheng Yu
main_finding: Systematises 139 paper families on semantic decision engines in network control loops: of 50 that claim to fit a control loop or time budget, four support the claim with matched measurement, and bounded tests show queueing can turn every isolated deadline hit into a miss.
